Q: Database design: to normalise or not? A:

Start by assuming pure normalization. Data integrity is always the highest priority.

Instead of jumping to denormalization, always check in this order:

  1. Indexes: Can I search faster? (Easiest fix).

  2. Caching: Can I avoid hitting the DB entirely? (Best fix).

  3. Materialized Views: Do I need to pre-calculate complex joins? (The safe denormalization).

    Only store JSON if you are treating it purely as a 'blob' or unstructured data (like logs/settings). If you ever need to search inside the JSON, you need to rethink the structure and build proper columns.

Q: golang error handling code example clarification A:

Let's unpack this switch statement:

switch u := any(e).(type) {
case interface{ Unwrap() error }:
    stack = append(stack, u.Unwrap())
case interface{ Unwrap() []error }:
    stack = append(stack, u.Unwrap()...)
}

This is called a type switch. If you are unfamiliar with type switches in general, see this chapter in the tour.

The switch expression any(e).(type)

any(e) converts e to type any. The .(type) switches on the dynamic type of any(e).

Since e is of type error, and error is an interface type, the type conversion is unnecessary. The switch statement simplifies to:

switch u := e.(type) {
// ...
}

The case expressions

The two cases use anonymous types. If we rewrite them with named types it is a bit easier to see what's going on:

type unwrapperOne interface {
    Unwrap() error
}
type unwrapperSlice interface {
    Unwrap() []error
}

switch u := e.(type) {
case unwrapperOne:
    stack = append(stack, u.Unwrap())
case unwrapperSlice:
    stack = append(stack, u.Unwrap()...)
}

So the type switch checks if e has one of the two Unwrap methods, and if so the unwrapped errors are appended to the stack.

What would trigger the second case statement?

Any value with an Unwrap []error method triggers the second case. Remember that error is an interface type. The concrete type can be whatever you want, so long as there is at least an Error() string method. You can add additional methods. errors.Join returns errors with such an Unwrap method, for instance.

What would happen if I feed it a non error (interface) type which doesnt even have an Unwrap() function?

If e doesn't have an Unwrap method, none of the cases match and execution simply continues after the switch statement.

Q: How to get a Scala singleton object from its fully qualified name using Scala reflection A:

Scala 2.13 ships with a scala-reflect runtime mirror that does exactly this. The key concept is that every Scala object — whether it's a companion or a standalone singleton — is a module in Scala's reflection vocabulary, so the same API the linked Stack Overflow answer uses for companions works here too.

Add the dependency (it's not on the default classpath):

libraryDependencies += "org.scala-lang" % "scala-reflect" % scalaVersion.value

Then:

import scala.reflect.runtime.universe
val mirror   = universe.runtimeMirror(getClass.getClassLoader)
val module   = mirror.staticModule("com.example.MyObject")   // ModuleSymbol
val instance = mirror.reflectModule(module).instance.asInstanceOf[MyTrait]

You can put together these in a method. I put an example here on Scastie for you to play around (the code lives in the built-in Playground module, which is why there's a discrepancy in naming).

What each step does, in terms that match the Scala source rather than the JVM encoding:

  • runtimeMirror(classLoader) builds a mirror against a specific classloader (use the one that can see your object).

  • staticModule("com.example.MyObject") looks up the module symbol by the same fully qualified name you write in source — no $ suffix, no knowledge of MODULE$.

  • reflectModule(module).instance returns the singleton value as Any; cast it to your trait.

If the name might be wrong or the class isn't on the classloader, staticModule throws ScalaReflectionException (and reflectModule can throw if the module's class isn't loadable), so wrap it in Try if you want to handle that gracefully.

A note on the distinction you drew: at the bytecode and reflection layer, "companion object" and "standalone object" are the same thing — both are emitted as a Foo$ class with a MODULE$ static field, and both are ModuleSymbols to scala-reflect. So the answers on the linked question apply directly; the companion-vs-standalone framing there is incidental.
